name: Kerma culture
title: The story of the Kerma culture

text: About 4,500 years ago, people built a walled village called Kerma, by the Nile in Sudan.
It grew into a big city, the capital of a strong Nubian kingdom.
src: c. 2500 BCE: A new fortified village at Kerma begins the Early Kerma period / Kerma, a town in northern Sudan in the part of ancient Nubia called Upper Nubia
Kerma grew from a fortified village into a city of about 25 hectares, the capital of a centralised Nubian kingdom that controlled the Nile from the First to the Fourth Cataract

text: Most people farmed in villages beside their fields, and others herded goats, sheep and cattle.
Kings lay under huge mounds with thousands of cattle skulls, and people were killed to be buried with them.
src: Most of its people lived in villages beside their fields, while some districts specialised in herding goats, sheep and cattle
the kings were buried under great tumuli in the city’s cemetery, with many human sacrifices / The royal tombs held the skulls of thousands of cattle

text: In the city’s centre stood the Western Deffufa, a huge mudbrick temple.
They honoured the ram, the lion, and a hippo and a giraffe with wings.
src: At the centre of the city stood the Western Deffufa, a large monumental temple of mudbrick
Four animals held the highest importance: the ram, the lion, the winged hippopotamus and the winged giraffe

text: Egypt, to the north, wanted Kerma’s gold, cattle, ivory, ebony and incense.
The two lands traded and fought, and Egypt’s king Senusret I built forts on the border.
src: Egypt coveted its gold, cattle, milk products, ebony, incense and ivory
it traded with Egypt and fought it / Senusret I built forts at Ikkur, Quban, Aniba, Buhen and Kor to guard the border

text: About 3,500 years ago, Kerma’s army of archers raided deep into Egypt.
Then an Egyptian king destroyed Kerma, but its people rebelled for about 200 years.
src: c. 1575–1550 BCE: Kerma, allied with the Hyksos, invades deep into Egypt / Kerma’s army was built around archers
Thutmose I of Egypt destroyed Kerma around 1504 BCE, but rebellions went on for two centuries

text: Later, the kings of Kush honoured Kerma as part of their past.
Statues of these later kings, found near Kerma, are now shown in the Kerma Museum.
src: the later Kingdom of Kush honoured Kerma as part of its past / the early Kushite kings used Kerma for royal burials and ceremonies
a cache of monumental black granite statues of the pharaohs of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, among them Taharqa and Tanutamun, now shown in the Kerma Museum
